items.title: Hijacking a Trusted LLM in Real-World Quantized Deployments Only Requires a Disguised Adapter
items.summary: QHijack-LoRA is an attack in which a third-party LoRA adapter behaves normally on the full-precision base model, passing audit, but hijacks decisions once the base is quantised for deployment. The attacker needs no changes to the base model or knowledge of the quantisation settings. The authors also propose a cross-precision paired audit that tests the adapter in its intended deployment configuration.
items.takeaway: Auditing a model in full precision does not prove its behaviour after quantisation. Third-party components should be tested in the exact configuration they will run in.

items.title: Fault Injection Attacks on Q-Learning: Analysis, Vulnerabilities, and Countermeasures
items.summary: The authors use voltage and clock glitching on a ChipWhisperer platform to attack several Q-learning implementations, showing that faults can corrupt rewards, Q-table values and actions. They find that Robust Q-learning does not stop NaN values persisting, and that triple modular redundancy protects copies of the table but not shared inputs such as the reward or the voting code. In a traffic simulator, one injected infinite value degraded waiting time by 148 times.
items.takeaway: Redundancy only helps when it covers every shared input and the voting logic itself, so a single unprotected reward path can defeat a protected model.

items.title: Protocol-Aware Auditing of Domain-Blind Feature Attribution in Network Intrusion Detection
items.summary: The authors show that feature-attribution explanations such as LIME and SHAP can query network states that break protocol rules, which makes their explanations unreliable for intrusion detection. Restricting the perturbations to rule-valid states (PA-LIME and related variants) reveals large variability that standard LIME hides. The paper also reports better attribution stability under adversarial perturbation with protocol repair.
items.takeaway: An explanation method is only trustworthy if its perturbations stay within the domain's valid states. Otherwise it may explain the model's behaviour on inputs that could never occur in production.

items.title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
items.summary: The authors ran SonarQube, Semgrep and language-specific analysers over twelve independent OCPP 1.6 charging station implementations, each in a different language. Findings ranged from two in Rust to 1,689 in Java, and the authors argue this mostly reflects how mature each language's SAST tooling is rather than how secure the code is. The study frames SAST tool choice as a factor when selecting languages for safety or security critical systems.
items.takeaway: Raw SAST finding counts measure tool coverage as much as code quality, so never compare security posture across languages using issue totals alone.

items.title: A Convex-Analytic Reformulation for Poisoning Attacks on Logistic Regression
items.summary: The paper studies poisoning attacks on L2-regularised logistic regression, where an attacker crafts the features of injected training points to maximise loss on clean data. Strong convexity of the defender's problem lets the authors replace the bilevel structure with a convex-analytic reformulation that leaves only bounded bilinear constraints. Solved with SCIP, this formulation yields substantially stronger dual bounds within a fixed time limit than local optimisation, which degrades performance on most datasets.
items.takeaway: When a defender's training objective is strongly convex, its first-order optimality conditions can turn a worst-case poisoning problem into a tractable optimisation with provable bounds, which is more useful for assessing risk than heuristic attack runs alone.

items.title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
items.summary: The paper estimates what share of a corpus was produced by a watermarked language model when documents may have been edited or paraphrased, using Gumbel-max and KGW watermarks. It gives a power envelope and finite-sample bounds that cover in resampling trials on OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B text. The authors show the bounds remain valid at 2,000 documents but lose exact-null coverage at 100,000 when the null error is around 0.01, while a calibrated null from an independent human sample keeps coverage.
items.takeaway: Small, harmless calibration errors can become decisive as sample size grows, so any statistical attribution or detection pipeline needs its null model validated at the scale it will actually be run.

items.title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
items.summary: The authors show that speech tokenizers, the front ends for ASR and audio-language models, can be disrupted by small perturbations at the semantic level. Their T-SemAttack uses an ensemble of semantic encoders to transfer attacks to unseen systems, and analysis points to shared adversarially sensitive input directions as the cause of transferability. They also propose ROSETok, a tokenizer trained with noise and robust distillation that improves downstream robustness.
items.takeaway: Attacks transfer between models when their gradients point in similar input directions, so using an ensemble of surrogate models is a practical way to build black-box attacks and to test defences.

items.title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search
items.summary: The authors present a multi-bit watermarking scheme that maps a short payload to a longer codeword, embeds it through logit biasing, and recovers it by nearest-codeword search using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. It recovers 16 to 24 bit payloads reliably on 200-token texts, but struggles with very short outputs, insertions and strong paraphrasing.
items.takeaway: Error-correcting codes can make a watermark recoverable from edited text, but each kind of edit (deletion, insertion, rewrite) needs its own robustness analysis.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
items.summary: The authors describe a ten-step workflow for using LLMs to help write machine-checked proofs in Dafny, covering specification, invariants, proof construction and solver performance tuning. They verified 37 algorithms, including the Hopcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, and conclude that the human role shifts toward supervision and specification review.
items.takeaway: Formal verification gains most from LLM help when the specification is kept rigorous and human-reviewed, since a proof is only as trustworthy as the statement it proves.
